html:
Recently we hosted Cyber Compliance in Rwanda: From Paperwork to Practice, a live conversation on what the BNR cyber security regulation in Rwanda actually requires, and where most institutions are still catching up.

Suleiman Wanekeya, Operations Manager at Sentinel Africa Consulting Group, was joined by Theogene Niyomamaza, Data Protection Manager at BPR Bank Rwanda, who stepped in as guest speaker after a scheduling conflict took our originally announced guest, Jean Pierre Nzabahimana, out of the session. Theogene brought close to a decade of experience across banking, telecom, and government, and it showed.

Here is what stood out.

1. The compliance deadline already passed

Regulation 50 of 2022 has been in force for a while now, and the transition period is over. As Suleiman put it early in the session, cyber security compliance is no longer a future consideration institutions can prepare for later. It has to be demonstrated now, whenever an audit or inspection happens.

2. Cyber security governance belongs to the board, not IT

One of the clearest points of the night. Suleiman was direct about it: “The regulation clearly says cyber security governance squarely lies with the board and the senior management. So when we find a gap, the first question is not to IT, it is supposed to be to the board.”

The reasoning is simple, IT teams cannot implement what they are not resourced to implement, and resourcing decisions sit with leadership. When a regulator finds a gap, the accountability question goes up, not down.

3. Most audit findings are not technical

Asked what keeps showing up across institutions, Suleiman named four recurring patterns. Policy documents that mention a requirement in a single shallow paragraph rather than actually addressing it. Penetration tests that are years overdue, or whose findings were never closed. Two hour incident notification requirements that exist on paper but have never actually been tested. And annual self-assessments that get copy pasted from the previous year rather than genuinely redone.

None of that is a technical failure. It is a follow-through failure, and it is exactly what shows up when a policy sits on a shelf.

4. Awareness training is chronically underfunded, and it is the one thing that undermines everything else

Suleiman called awareness “the backbone of everything.” If staff do not know who to call when something goes wrong, none of the rest of the implementation work matters. Theogene added a practical nuance, awareness should not be one generic session for the whole organisation, marketing needs a different conversation than IT does.

5. Start with a risk based approach, not everything at once

For institutions that already know they have gaps, Theogene’s advice was to resist the urge to fix everything simultaneously. Identify your assets and data first, run a proper risk or vulnerability assessment, classify what you find by criticality, and work the highest risk items first. Suleiman added that this only works if there is a governance structure, a steering committee reporting to the board, actually reviewing that risk exposure on an ongoing basis.

What the room told us

We ran a few live polls during the session, and the results were worth sharing on their own.

  • 80 percent of attendees described their institution as fully compliant, while the remaining 20 percent said they had not yet formally assessed their compliance
  • Most attendees had run a cyber security assessment or vulnerability scan within the last year, though a meaningful number had last done one over a year ago
  • On confidence in passing a BNR inspection today, most said very confident or somewhat confident, a genuinely encouraging sign, though as Suleiman noted, confidence and evidence are not always the same thing

The line that summed it up

Theogene closed with a distinction worth holding onto: “Let’s be more driven by resilience, other than being driven by compliance.” Not because compliance does not matter, but because institutions that build for resilience tend to pass compliance reviews as a byproduct, while institutions that build only for compliance often cannot show their work when it counts.

We have pulled two of the deeper threads from this conversation into standalone pieces, what auditors actually find when they walk into a Rwandan bank or MFI, and the governance gap that keeps showing up between boards and IT teams, both worth a read if this recap raised more questions than it answered.

Our next session, on Business Continuity, is coming in September. If you would like to be part of that conversation, or want support closing any of the gaps discussed above, reach the Rwanda team at Plot KG688 Street, Kacyiru, Kigali, or on +250 782 746 073.
